procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 05.09.2000 in Criminal Appeal Nos. 26 and 25 of 2000
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Not Applicable. The case originated in the Supreme Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court initially heard Criminal Appeals 25-26 of 2000, resulting in the Judgment and Order dated 05.09.2000. Subsequently, a Review Petition (Criminal) Nos. 1139-1140 of 2000 was filed. Later, a writ petition, W.P. (Criminal) No. 126 of 2013, was filed and dismissed on 12th August 2013. Criminal Miscellaneous Petition No. 157334 of 2018 was filed in the Review Petition. Several I.A.s were filed, including I.A. No. 5242 of 2016 and I.A. No. 5245 of 2016, seeking to reopen the review petition. Crl. M.P. No. 155609 of 2019 was filed by an intervenor objecting to an inquiry report. An inquiry was directed in an order passed on 29th January 2019 based on materials disclosed in an application.

issue.issue_text: Whether the applications (I.A. No. 5242 of 2016 and I.A. No. 5245 of 2016) for reopening the review petition should be allowed.

facts: The applicant filed two applications, I.A. No. 5242 of 2016 and I.A. No. 5245 of 2016, seeking to reopen a review petition.
The applicant also had a separate application before the court under Section 9(2) of the 2015 Act regarding a plea of juvenility.
law: An application under Section 9(2) of the 2015 Act is considered an independent legal proceeding.
application: The Court viewed the application under Section 9(2) of the 2015 Act as a distinct and separate proceeding from the earlier review petition.
Because it was an independent proceeding, the Court could decide the juvenility issue raised in that application on its own merits.
This meant the Court did not need to go back and reopen the previous review order to address the applicant's claim.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the applications to reopen the review petition because it found them unnecessary. The Court decided the applicant's claim under a separate, independent proceeding (an application under Section 9(2) of the 2015 Act) without needing to revisit the original review order.

issue.issue_text: Whether the application under Section 9(2) of the 2015 Act, treated as an independent proceeding, should be allowed.

facts: An application was filed under Section 9(2) of the Juvenile Justice Act, 2015, claiming the applicant was a juvenile at the time of the offense.
This claim was made after the applicant's conviction and sentence had been confirmed and his review petition had been dismissed by the Supreme Court.
A previous writ petition raising the same plea had been dismissed 'in limine' (without a reasoned order).
The Court directed a Principal District and Sessions Judge to conduct an inquiry into the applicant's age.
The inquiry relied on a school certificate which indicated the applicant was 12 years and 6 months old when the crime was committed.
law: An application under Section 9(2) of the 2015 Act is an independent proceeding and can be raised before any court at any stage, even after the final disposal of the case.
The dismissal of a prior writ petition 'in limine' does not act as res judicata (a bar) to a subsequent statutory application under Section 9(2).

When a court conducts an inquiry into juvenility under Section 9(2), it is not required to scrupulously follow the formal trial procedure stipulated in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, and the Indian Evidence Act, 1872.
The court can formulate its own procedure for such an inquiry.
The law applicable for determining the procedure for a juvenility claim is the law in force at the time of the inquiry (in this case, the 2015 Act).
application: The Court first established that the application was maintainable. It held that the statutory right under Section 9(2) to raise a juvenility plea at any time was not barred by the earlier dismissal of the writ petition without a reasoned order.
The Court treated the application as a separate and independent proceeding, distinct from the earlier review petition.

It then examined the procedure of the inquiry conducted by the Sessions Judge and found no flaw. It reasoned that since the 2015 Act does not mandate a specific procedure for a court-led inquiry (unlike one by a Juvenile Justice Board), the fact-finding approach taken by the Inquiring Judge was permissible.

Finally, the Court accepted the school certificate as valid evidence, noting that the school's admission register was maintained in the ordinary course of business. Based on this certificate, the Court determined that the applicant was indeed a juvenile (12 years and 6 months old) on the date the offense was committed.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted and allowed the application, concluding that it was a valid, independent proceeding. Based on the evidence from the inquiry it had ordered, the Court found that the applicant was a juvenile at the time of the offense, which by operation of law invalidated the death sentence that had been previously imposed.

issue.issue_text: The objection raised by the intervenor to the inquiry report in Crl. M.P. No. 155609 of 2019.

facts: An intervenor filed Crl. M.P. No. 155609 of 2019, raising an objection to an inquiry report.
The inquiry report, prepared by an 'Inquiring Judge', had sustained an applicant's claim of juvenility.
The intervenor's counsel argued for the rejection of this report.
application: The Supreme Court explicitly stated that it had considered the content of the intervenor's petition.
The Court examined the process followed by the Inquiring Judge and found "no flaw in the procedure which has been adopted".
reasoning.conclusion: Because the Court considered the intervenor's arguments but found no flaws in the inquiry's procedure, it disposed of the petition, effectively rejecting the objection to the report.

issue.issue_text: The validity of the legal principle laid down in the precedent reported in [2006] 10 Suppl. SCR 988.

law.text: The primary legal precedent under review was the principle established in the case reported in [2006] 10 Suppl. SCR 988.
The Court used the principles from the case reported in [2012] 10 SCR 540 as a basis for its decision.

application.text: The Supreme Court directly assessed the legal principle laid down in the precedent [2006] 10 Suppl. SCR 988.
The Court concluded that this precedent was 'not good law,' thereby invalidating the legal principle it contained.
In reaching this conclusion, the Court relied on the legal reasoning established in the case of [2012] 10 SCR 540.
The Court also distinguished several other cases, indicating that their legal circumstances or principles were not applicable to the current issue.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the validity of the legal principle from [2006] 10 Suppl. SCR 988 by explicitly holding that the precedent was 'not good law'.

issue.issue_text: The applicability of the precedents reported in [2016] 2 SCR 1089, [2008] 14 SCR 161, and [2001] 3 SCR 669 to the present case.

facts: The provided text is a list of case law citations and does not contain the specific facts of the case being decided.
law: When a court "distinguishes" a precedent, it means the court finds that the legal reasoning or the facts of the previous case are different from the current case. Therefore, the rule from the previous case does not apply to the current one.
application: The Supreme Court explicitly reviewed the three precedents mentioned in the issue.
The case of *Ramdeo Chauhan alias Raj Nath v. State of Assam* ([2001] 3 SCR 669) was 'distinguished' at Paragraph 14.
The case of *Parag Bhati (Juvenile) v. State of Uttar Pradesh* ([2016] 2 SCR 1089) was 'distinguished' at Paragraph 32.
The case of *Babloo Pasi v. State of Jharkhand* ([2008] 14 SCR 161) was 'distinguished' at Paragraph 37.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the applicability of the three precedents by distinguishing them from the present case. This means the Court determined that the factual circumstances or legal principles in those prior cases were not sufficiently similar to be binding or persuasive in the current matter.

cases.case_name: Ashwani Kumar Saxena v. State of Madhya Pradesh
cases.principle: The inquiry into a claim of juvenility is an inquiry under the JJ Act following the procedure under Rule 12, not a trial following the procedure laid down under the Criminal Procedure Code.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The provided text does not contain a binding legal rule. It consists of case citations, procedural history, and an introductory phrase indicating that a summary of judgments is forthcoming, but the summary itself is not included in the text.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court allowed the application raising the plea of juvenility, treating it as an independent proceeding under the 2015 Act. The court accepted the findings of an inquiry report establishing the appellant's juvenility at the time of the offense, noting that this plea was raised as an additional ground and did not constitute a challenge to the jurisdiction of the trial court or the validity of the conviction itself.
legal_tests_applied: The court applied the doctrine of 'parens patriae', which obligates the courts to act as a guardian for minors who, due to legal disability, require protection. This doctrine imposes a duty on courts, Juvenile Justice Boards, and Committees to actively seek evidence to determine juvenility, as specified in rules like Rule 12(3)(a)(i) to (iii) of the Juvenile Justice Rules.
why_appellant_lost: The court highlighted a limitation in the appellant's plea, clarifying that it was not a challenge to the conviction on jurisdictional grounds: "there was and is no challenge to the order of conviction recorded by the courts below in this case either before the High Court or before us. As a matter of fact the plea of juvenility before this Court by way of an additional ground stopped short of challenging the conviction of the appellant on the ground that the court concerned had no jurisdiction to try the appellant."

The appellant's applications (I.A. No. 5242 of 2016 and I.A. No. 5245 of 2016) to reopen the review petition were rejected, though the specific reasoning for this rejection is not provided in the supplied text.
why_respondent_won: The respondent's arguments against the juvenility claim failed because the legal precedents they relied upon were systematically dismantled by the court. The court held that the legal principle from the precedent in [2006] 10 Suppl. SCR 988 was 'not good law'. Furthermore, the court distinguished the other precedents cited ([2016] 2 SCR 1089, [2008] 14 SCR 161, and [2001] 3 SCR 669), finding them inapplicable to the facts and circumstances of the present case.
policy_considerations: The court articulated a broad policy consideration regarding the justice system's duty towards minors, stating: "We also remind all courts/Juvenile Justice Boards and the Committees functioning under the Act that a duty is cast on them to seek evidence by obtaining the certificate, etc. mentioned in Rules 12(3)(a)(i) to (iii). The courts in such situations act as a parens patriae because they have a kind of guardianship over minors who from their legal disability stand in need of protection."
